questions.q: Which of these is a real reason organizations replicate data across clouds, according to this lesson?
options: To avoid ever having to think about data gravity again
Because every cloud provider requires at least two copies of all data by law
Disaster recovery, low-latency reads for distributed users, compliance/sovereignty requirements, or deliberate multi-cloud redundancy
To make egress costs disappear
questions.explain: Cross-cloud replication is taken on for specific reasons -- disaster recovery, serving distributed users with lower latency, meeting compliance/sovereignty needs, or deliberate redundancy against vendor dependence -- not by default.

questions.q: What does change data capture (CDC) actually do?
options: It reads a database's transaction log and streams every insert, update, and delete as an event, used to replicate changes into another cloud
It encrypts a database at rest
It compresses a dataset before storage
It deletes stale records automatically after 30 days
questions.explain: CDC tools like Debezium, AWS DMS, or Azure Data Factory's change-tracking pipelines read the transaction log (not the live tables) and stream each change as an event to a target system, often in another cloud.

questions.q: Why is dual-writing from the application layer (writing to two databases in two clouds within the same request) considered risky?
options: It is actually the safest and most recommended replication pattern
It is illegal under most data protection regulations
It always runs faster than any dedicated replication mechanism
A partial failure -- one write succeeds, the other times out -- leaves the two copies silently inconsistent with no systematic way to detect or repair it
questions.explain: Dedicated replication mechanisms are built to handle partial failure, ordering, and retries correctly; hand-rolled dual writes from application code generally are not, and a partial failure leaves copies silently diverged.

questions.q: Why do cross-cloud replication systems generally use eventual consistency rather than strict consistency?
options: Eventual consistency is required by GDPR
Strict consistency is technically impossible to implement in any database
Strict consistency across clouds would require every write to wait for acknowledgment from a replica possibly tens or hundreds of milliseconds away, which is prohibitively expensive at scale
Eventual consistency is only used for test environments, never production
questions.explain: Enforcing strict consistency across real network latency between clouds/regions would mean every write pays that latency cost, which is why essentially every cross-cloud replication system instead accepts eventual consistency.

questions.q: What is last-writer-wins (LWW), as used by default in Cosmos DB and DynamoDB Global Tables?
options: A backup scheduling policy
A conflict-resolution policy that keeps the update with the latest timestamp and discards the other when the same record is written in two places
A pricing tier for high-availability storage
A network routing algorithm for choosing the nearest region
questions.explain: LWW is a conflict-resolution policy for multi-writer scenarios: when the same record is updated in two locations near-simultaneously, the update with the later timestamp is kept and the other is silently discarded.
